solution:
Put \(x=\frac{\pi}{2}+h\), so that \(h \to 0\) as \(x \to \frac{\pi}{2}\). Then \(\cot x=\cot\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+h\right)=-\tan h\) and \(\pi-2x=\pi-2\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+h\right)=-2h\). Hence
\(\lim\limits_{x \to \frac{\pi}{2}} f(x)=\lim\limits_{h \to 0}\frac{2^{-\tan h}-1}{-2h}=\lim\limits_{h \to 0}\left[\frac{2^{-\tan h}-1}{-\tan h}\cdot\frac{-\tan h}{-2h}\right]\).
Using \(\lim\limits_{u \to 0}\frac{2^{u}-1}{u}=\log 2\) (with \(u=-\tan h \to 0\)) and \(\lim\limits_{h \to 0}\frac{\tan h}{h}=1\), this equals \(\log 2 \times \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}\log 2=\log 2^{1/2}=\log\sqrt{2}\).
Since \(f\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=\log\sqrt{2}\) is exactly this limit, \(f\) is continuous at \(x=\frac{\pi}{2}\). Option D is wrong because the limit is \(\log\sqrt{2}\), not \(2\log 3\); B and C are ruled out since the limit exists and equals the assigned value.
why: The limit works out to \(\frac{1}{2}\log 2=\log\sqrt{2}\), which is precisely the value assigned at \(x=\frac{\pi}{2}\).

solution:
For continuity, \(f\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\lim\limits_{x \to \frac{\pi}{4}} f(x)\). Put \(x=\frac{\pi}{4}+h\), so \(h \to 0\).
Then \(\sin x=\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{4}+h\right)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\cos h+\sin h)\), so \(\sqrt{2}\sin x=\cos h+\sin h\) and the numerator becomes \(1-\cos h-\sin h\). The denominator is \(\pi-4\left(\frac{\pi}{4}+h\right)=-4h\).
Hence \(\lim\limits_{h \to 0}\frac{(1-\cos h)-\sin h}{-4h}=\lim\limits_{h \to 0}\left[\frac{1-\cos h}{-4h}-\frac{\sin h}{-4h}\right]\).
Since \(\lim\limits_{h \to 0}\frac{1-\cos h}{h}=0\) and \(\lim\limits_{h \to 0}\frac{\sin h}{h}=1\), the value is \(0+\frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{4}\).
Therefore \(f\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\frac{1}{4}\).
why: After the substitution \(x=\frac{\pi}{4}+h\) the numerator behaves like \(-h\) against a denominator \(-4h\), giving \(\frac{1}{4}\).

solution:
Write the quotient so that each factor is a standard limit:
\(\frac{(\sin 2x)\tan 5x}{(e^{2x}-1)^2}=\frac{\sin 2x}{2x}\cdot\frac{\tan 5x}{5x}\cdot\left(\frac{2x}{e^{2x}-1}\right)^{2}\cdot\frac{(2x)(5x)}{(2x)^{2}}\).
As \(x \to 0\), \(\frac{\sin 2x}{2x} \to 1\), \(\frac{\tan 5x}{5x} \to 1\) and \(\frac{e^{2x}-1}{2x} \to 1\), while the algebraic factor is \(\frac{10x^{2}}{4x^{2}}=\frac{10}{4}=\frac{5}{2}\).
Hence \(\lim\limits_{x \to 0} f(x)=\frac{5}{2}\), so \(f(0)=\frac{5}{2}\).
Note that \(e\) does not survive in the answer at all: \(e^{2x}-1\) behaves like \(2x\), so options A and B are ruled out on principle.
why: Replacing each factor by its linear order gives \(\frac{(2x)(5x)}{(2x)^2}=\frac{5}{2}\).

solution:
Factorise the denominator: \(x^{2}+2x-8=(x+4)(x-2)\), which vanishes at \(x=-4\) and \(x=2\). The numerator \(x^{2}-7x+10=(x-2)(x-5)\) also vanishes at \(x=2\), but that is irrelevant here because the domain is restricted.
The function is defined only on \([-6,-3]\). Of the two zeros of the denominator, \(x=2 \notin [-6,-3]\) while \(x=-4 \in [-6,-3]\).
So within the given domain the only point of discontinuity is \(x=-4\).
Option A and D name \(x=2\), which lies outside the interval, and C names \(x=0\), where the denominator is \(-8 \ne 0\).
why: Of the denominator's two zeros \(-4\) and \(2\), only \(-4\) lies in the stated domain \([-6,-3]\).

solution:
First read the domains. \(|x-1| \ge 3\) means \(x-1 \ge 3\) or \(x-1 \le -3\), i.e. \(x \ge 4\) or \(x \le -2\); the linear piece \(4x+5\) holds on \(-2<x<4\). So the two junction points are \(x=-2\) and \(x=4\).
Continuity at \(x=-2\): \(a(-2)^{2}+b(-2)+1=4(-2)+5\), i.e. \(4a-2b+1=-3\), so \(4a-2b=-4\), i.e. \(2a-b=-2\).
Continuity at \(x=4\): \(4(4)+5=a(4)^{2}+b(4)+1\), i.e. \(21=16a+4b+1\), so \(16a+4b=20\), i.e. \(4a+b=5\).
Adding \(2a-b=-2\) and \(4a+b=5\) gives \(6a=3\), so \(a=\frac{1}{2}\), and then \(b=5-4a=5-2=3\).
Check: \(2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)-3=-2\) and \(4\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+3=5\), both satisfied.
why: Matching the pieces at both junctions \(x=-2\) and \(x=4\) gives \(2a-b=-2\) and \(4a+b=5\), so \(a=\frac{1}{2},\ b=3\).

solution:
Divide numerator and denominator by \(x^{2}\) and use \(\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\frac{a^{x}-1}{x}=\log a\):
\(k=\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\frac{\left(\frac{16^{x}-1}{x}\right)\left(\frac{9^{x}-1}{x}\right)}{\left(\frac{27^{x}-1}{x}\right)\left(\frac{32^{x}-1}{x}\right)}=\frac{(\log 16)(\log 9)}{(\log 27)(\log 32)}\).
Now \(\log 16=4\log 2\), \(\log 9=2\log 3\), \(\log 27=3\log 3\), \(\log 32=5\log 2\), so
\(k=\frac{(4\log 2)(2\log 3)}{(3\log 3)(5\log 2)}=\frac{8\log 2\log 3}{15\log 3\log 2}=\frac{8}{15}\).
Every factor here is positive, so the negative alternative \(-\frac{8}{15}\) is excluded on sign alone.
why: Reducing every logarithm to \(\log 2\) and \(\log 3\) makes them cancel, leaving \(\frac{4\times 2}{3\times 5}=\frac{8}{15}\).

solution:
Factorise both parts. Since \(32^{x}=(8\times 4)^{x}=8^{x}\cdot 4^{x}\),
\(32^{x}-8^{x}-4^{x}+1=8^{x}4^{x}-8^{x}-4^{x}+1=(8^{x}-1)(4^{x}-1)\).
Also \(4^{x}-2^{x+1}+1=(2^{x})^{2}-2\cdot 2^{x}+1=(2^{x}-1)^{2}\).
Hence
\(k=\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\frac{(8^{x}-1)(4^{x}-1)}{(2^{x}-1)^{2}}=\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\frac{\frac{8^{x}-1}{x}\cdot\frac{4^{x}-1}{x}}{\left(\frac{2^{x}-1}{x}\right)^{2}}=\frac{(\log 8)(\log 4)}{(\log 2)^{2}}=\frac{(3\log 2)(2\log 2)}{(\log 2)^{2}}=6\).
The logarithms cancel completely, so the answer is a pure number and options C and D are excluded.

Since \(12^{x}=4^{x}\cdot 3^{x}\), the numerator factorises:
\(12^{x}-4^{x}-3^{x}+1=4^{x}3^{x}-4^{x}-3^{x}+1=(4^{x}-1)(3^{x}-1)\).
The denominator is \(1-\cos 2x=2\sin^{2}x\).
Therefore
\(f(0)=\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\frac{(4^{x}-1)(3^{x}-1)}{2\sin^{2}x}=\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\frac{\frac{4^{x}-1}{x}\cdot\frac{3^{x}-1}{x}}{2\left(\frac{\sin x}{x}\right)^{2}}=\frac{(\log 4)(\log 3)}{2}=\frac{(2\log 2)(\log 3)}{2}=\log 2 \cdot \log 3\).
Option C, \(\frac{\log 2 \cdot \log 3}{2}\), is what one gets by forgetting that \(\log 4=2\log 2\); the factor \(2\) cancels the \(2\) from \(1-\cos 2x=2\sin^{2}x\).

Take logarithms: \(\log f(x)=\frac{4}{x}\left[\log(4+5x)-\log(4-7x)\right]=\frac{4}{x}\left[\log\left(1+\frac{5x}{4}\right)-\log\left(1-\frac{7x}{4}\right)\right]\).
Using \(\lim\limits_{u \to 0}\frac{\log(1+u)}{u}=1\),
\(\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\frac{\log\left(1+\frac{5x}{4}\right)}{x}=\frac{5}{4}\) and \(\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\frac{\log\left(1-\frac{7x}{4}\right)}{x}=-\frac{7}{4}\).
Hence \(\lim\limits_{x \to 0}\log f(x)=4\left[\frac{5}{4}+\frac{7}{4}\right]=4 \times 3=12\), so \(k=e^{12}\).
Note the base is \(\frac{4+5x}{4-7x} \to 1\) and the index \(\frac{4}{x} \to \infty\), so this is genuinely the \(1^{\infty}\) form and the exponential answer is expected.

The greatest integer function \(\lfloor x \rfloor\) is a step function which is continuous at every non-integer point and discontinuous at every integer, because there the left-hand and right-hand limits differ by \(1\).
The domain here is the open interval \((-1,2)\). The integers lying strictly inside it are \(0\) and \(1\); the endpoints \(-1\) and \(2\) are not in the domain, so continuity is not even defined there.
Check at \(x=0\): \(\lim\limits_{x \to 0^{-}}\lfloor x \rfloor=-1\) while \(\lim\limits_{x \to 0^{+}}\lfloor x \rfloor=0\), so \(f\) is discontinuous.
Check at \(x=1\): \(\lim\limits_{x \to 1^{-}}\lfloor x \rfloor=0\) while \(\lim\limits_{x \to 1^{+}}\lfloor x \rfloor=1\), again discontinuous.
So \(f\) is discontinuous exactly at \(x=0\) and \(x=1\).
why: Only the integers strictly inside the open interval \((-1,2)\) count, and those are \(0\) and \(1\).
